articles.title: King Charles and family mark 60th anniversary of Aberfan disaster
articles.summary: King Charles, accompanied by his ​wife and son, will visit south Wales on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster which killed 144 people.
articles.body: LONDON — King Charles III led tributes Wednesday to the people of the Welsh village of Aberfan on the 60th anniversary of a coal slide onto a school that claimed the lives of 116 children and 28 adults. Charles, who was joined in Aberfan by his wife Queen Camilla and his eldest son Prince William, said it was “profoundly humbling” to hear the testimonies of those who survived the collapse of a mountain of coal sludge onto Pantglas Junior School on Oct. 21 1966. The disaster unfolded following days of heavy rain, when excavated mining debris from the nearby Merthyr Vale Colliery was dislodged and came thundering down the hillside. The coal waste had been piled high above Aberfan for years, even though there were numerous underground springs below. Children in the school were just getting ready for lessons when 1.5 million cubic feet of liquefied slurry crashed into the school and a number of nearby houses. About half the children from the junior school died in the tragedy. The coal executives at the time had been warned about the possibility of a debris slide prior to the disaster. Despite a 76-day public inquiry at the time, no one faced prosecution or lost their job. “We have heard stories of heartbreak, but also of heroism,” Charles said while visiting the Aberfan Memorial Garden, which is located on the site of the junior school, “We have heard of the most agonizing grief, but also of the most inspiring grace.” During the memorial events, a prayer and a moment of silence were held in the garden. The king and William laid wreaths, while the queen placed a posy. “No one should ever have to bear what you, as a community, have endured, but no one could have borne it with greater strength, resilience, or hope,” Charles said. “Please know how deeply we feel with your sorrow, how greatly we admire your strength, and how you will, always, be in our hearts.” Rona Price, 94, a former policewoman who attended the scene of the tragedy, was among those who met the royals, describing it as a “great honor.” Aberfan survivor Jeff Edwards thanked the royal family for their “enduring support, compassion and commitment” in a speech to those gathered at the community center. The royals have long showed their support for the community. Charles’ mother, Queen Elizabeth II, visited Aberfan eight days after the tragedy and shortly after a mass funeral had taken place. Her decision not to visit sooner was said to have been one of the greatest regrets of her reign. She returned to Aberfan three more times during her life. “October 21 1966 is forever etched into our memory, a day of unimaginable tragedy and loss that changed the lives of families and the community forever,” Edwards said. “The presence of members of the royal family in those difficult years became a lasting and deeply valued part of Aberfan’s history.” Earlier this week, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham also visited the village to pay tribute to the strength and resilience of the community in the aftermath of the disaster. “I visited on Monday and heard how the injustices people suffered at the time and in the aftermath of the tragedy at the hands of the state still hurt,” he said Wednesday in the House of Commons.

articles.title: Aberfan disaster: Royal Family pay respects to 'most tragic of days imaginable'
articles.summary: In total 116 children and 28 adults were killed when a colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.
articles.body:
The King has described the Aberfan disaster which killed 116 children and 28 adults as the "most tragic of days imaginable" on its 60th anniversary.

Pantglas Junior School and a number of nearby houses in the village near Merthyr Tydfil, south Wales, were catastrophically engulfed in coal slurry after the colliery spoil tip collapsed on 21 October 1966.

King Charles III, Queen Camilla and the Prince of Wales joined survivors and bereaved families on Wednesday and laid wreaths and a posy with the last surviving teacher in the Aberfan Memorial Garden, located on the site of the school.

The King also paid tribute to the community's strength, resilience and "unconquerable spirit".

Warning: This story contains upsetting details that some may find distressing

About half the children from the school died when excavated mining debris from the Merthyr Vale Colliery was dislodged, and 150,000 tonnes of coal waste came thundering down the hillside.

Emergency services, miners and people who rushed to the village began an around-the-clock battle to dig out those trapped by the debris.

An official inquiry found the National Coal Board was responsible for the disaster, but no-one has ever been prosecuted.

On Friday morning a minute's silence was held at 09:15 BST to mark the moment the coal spoil struck the village, and church bells rang 144 times for each child and adult who died.

Pupils at Ynysowen Community Primary School, which was built to carry on the legacy of Pantglas, also gathered to pay their respects.

The royals joined survivors, bereaved parents and members of the community in the memorial garden to pay tribute to all those who lost their lives, followed by a visit to the nearby Aberfan and Merthyr Vale Community Centre.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth also greeted crowds of people in Aberfan, with flowers that Aberfan victims would have seen in their gardens chosen for the wreaths laid in the garden.

Who was responsible for the Aberfan disaster?

The coal waste had been piled high on the side of Mynydd Merthyr – above Aberfan – for years, even though there were numerous underground springs below.

An official inquiry in 1967 found the National Coal Board was responsible for the Aberfan disaster, but survivors and bereaved families have long pointed to a litany of injustices.

Money was taken from the public disaster fund to help pay for the removal of remaining coal tips above the village, while compensation payments were limited and survivors had to undergo repeated assessments.

Support to help deal with their trauma was also minimal.

Professor Iain McLean, the co-author of Aberfan - Government and Disaster, has questioned why nobody was ever prosecuted for the Aberfan disaster.

Speaking on the BBC Radio Wales Phone In on Wednesday, he said: "And so one of the other failures of the government of the day is their, to me, incomprehensible failure to sack Lord Robens and his senior directors."

Robens was the chairman of the National Coal Board at the time, and had faced numerous complaints about the dangers that loomed a quarter of a mile high above the village.

One of these included a petition from Pantglas school in 1963, three years before the disaster.

In 1997, McLean met three of the counsels who had appeared before the 1967 tribunal and asked why no legal action was taken.

"They all said 'nobody thought of it at the time'," he said.

On Wednesday the royal party met retired members of the emergency services at the community centre who helped in the hours and days after the disaster.

They then spent time with survivors, bereaved parents, and siblings of those who died.

In a speech to those in the community centre, King Charles said the disaster "was and always will be, the saddest and most tragic of days imaginable".

He said: "Over the years, as once again today, it has been profoundly humbling to hear the testimonies of survivors of relatives who lost their loved ones, and of rescuers who fought so hard to save others during this appalling tragedy."

"Today in our nation and across the world, thoughts will turn to you in Aberfan, hearts far from this valley will ache with yours."

King Charles added: "Throughout all this, and through all the years, your unconquerable spirit has shone all the more brightly for the darkness which it has overcome.

"No one should ever have to bear what you, as a community, have endured, but no one could have borne it with greater strength, resilience, or hope.

"Please know how deeply we feel with your sorrow, how greatly we admire your strength, and how you will, always, be in our hearts."

Jeff Edwards, who survived the disaster as an eight-year-old pupil , said in a speech that October 21 1966 was "forever etched into our memory, a day of unimaginable tragedy and loss that changed the lives of families and the community forever".

"Yet, amidst the terrible sorrow, we were comforted by those who came to stand with us to share our grief and offer their support," he said.

"The presence of members of the royal family in those difficult years became a lasting and deeply valued part of Aberfan's history."

Prince William also visited Ynysowen Community Primary School to unveil an Aberfan Memorial Tree.

The tree was designed and created by ArtMetal, a family-run metalwork company based in Rhayader, Powys.

The concept was developed by school headteacher Simone Roden, along with Edwards who is vice chair of governors at the school.

During the early planning stages, pupils helped shape the vision of the memorial by sharing drawings and ideas.

During the visit, Prince William met pupils and heard them recite poems they had written about the disaster and read memories recorded by the children who survived.

"Well done guys," William told the pupils.

"It shows the next generation does care about them, and it matters."

Before unveiling the sculpture, he watched the pupils perform the Aberfan Song and well-known children's song Everyone Belongs.

articles.title: The best vacuum sealers to keep food fresh longer, according to experts
articles.summary: Vacuum sealers keep food fresh for longer and help prevent freezer burn. Food experts explain how to use them and what to look for, plus top-rated picks from Nesco, Anova and more.
articles.body: If you’ve ever had to toss a freezer-burned chicken breast or pricey steak, then you know the true cost of food waste — a vacuum sealer can help. By removing air before sealing, these gadgets slow spoilage and keep meat, produce and leftovers fresh longer. This kitchen gadget also makes it easier to buy in bulk and meal prep. In fact, many people say that the machines practically pay for themselves by cutting back on food waste, which saves you money in the long run. To find out if this is true, I spoke to food experts about the benefits of vacuum sealers and how to use them properly. I also rounded up highly-rated options, including compact handheld models and heavy-duty machines that can take care of large jobs. The best vacuum sealers for storing food To round up the best food vacuum sealers, I used expert guidance (more on that below) on what to look for in one of these kitchen devices. Each item below has at least a four-star average rating from 500 or more shoppers at Amazon and other retailers. This countertop sealer from Nesco has three seal settings (dry, moist and double), plus normal and gentle vacuum pressures so softer foods don’t get crushed. A pulse function gives you manual control over suction for delicate items like pastries and cut produce. It also has built-in roll storage and a bag cutter for making custom sizes. It works with any brand of vacuum sealer bags. Anova is best known for its sous vide cookers, and this compact sealer is a natural companion if you cook that way. Not in the know? Sous vide is a cooking technique where food is sealed in an airtight pouch and cooked in a temperature-controlled water bath for an extended period. This sealer is simple to operate, with a single button that removes air and seals the bag. Separate pulse and seal buttons give you more control when you’re working with delicate foods. Plus, its small footprint makes it easy to stash in a drawer or cabinet. This countertop sealer has two vacuum pumps, so it pulls air out quickly, even with larger items, according to the brand. It offers multiple food modes plus gentle and normal vacuum strengths for delicate foods. A removable drip tray catches liquid and is easy to wash. It also has built-in roll storage, a bag cutter and an auto-locking handle you can operate with one hand. If you want a sealer that does most of the work for you, this compact model from Fresko is what you need. It detects the bag automatically once you insert it, then vacuums and seals without you pressing down the lid. For soft or juicy foods, the pulse button switches to manual mode to help you avoid crushing those items. If you’re short on counter space, this handheld system from Zwilling is a compact alternative to a bulky countertop machine. Its cordless, rechargeable pump removes air at the press of a button and shuts off automatically once the bag or container is sealed. The starter set comes with two vacuum containers, four reusable zip-top bags and the pump. The containers and bags are dishwasher-safe and the bags are microwave-safe once unsealed. What are the benefits of a vacuum sealer for food? The main benefit of a vacuum sealer is that it helps food last longer while keeping its quality intact — particularly when freezing it. According to experts, when food is exposed to air, it’s more likely to dry out, lose flavor and develop freezer burn. “Vacuum sealing can greatly increase the quality of your stored items,” says Kara Brown, a recipe developer and beekeeper. “The length of time it allows you to freeze foods will be approximately double or triple that of non-vacuum packed foods as there is less air and therefore less potential for freezer burn.” That’s especially useful for pricier proteins you may be freezing. Removing air also helps preserve how food looks and tastes. “The air isn’t getting at the food, oxidization is slowed down, and you get fewer flavor and color changes,” says Christine Pittman, founder and CEO at TheCookful and CookForTwo, both of which send meal plans and recipes straight to your inbox. “Everything just keeps for longer. Sometimes for two to three times as long.” Vacuum-sealed bags are also more compact than bulky containers or loosely wrapped packages, so they free up space in your freezer. “It also helps you organize your freezer better because you could stack your freezer bags laying flat and then you can get more of them in there,” says Pittman. How do food vacuum sealers work? Most vacuum sealers for home use are countertop models called external or edge sealers. To use one, you place food in a specially designed plastic bag and insert the open end into the machine. A pump then pulls the air out of the bag, and once most of it is removed, a heated strip melts the plastic together to create an airtight seal around the food. These sealers typically require textured or embossed bags, which have channels that let air escape during the vacuuming process. Many models also have a pulse function that gives you more control over how much air is removed, which helps keep delicate items like bread or berries from getting crushed. How I picked the best vacuum sealers for food To help pick the best vacuum sealers for food, I asked experts what to consider when shopping. Here is what they said: Size: Countertop vacuum sealers can take up a fair amount of space, so measure your counter or cabinet before buying and consider where you’ll store the machine between uses. Also check the width of the sealing strip, since it determines the largest bag you can use. If you’re sealing big cuts of meat or bulk purchases, a wider strip is helpful, while a compact or handheld model may be enough if you mostly seal leftovers or smaller portions.Storage bags: “Find out ahead of time if the vacuum sealer will work with different brands of bags or if you have to buy their specific brand,” says Pittman. “If you have to buy their brand, you’ll want to think about how expensive they are.” Some models also work with bag rolls you cut to size, which can reduce waste and let you customize bags for different foods.Price: Handheld sealers are generally the most affordable, followed by countertop edge sealers. Think about how often you’ll use it: If you vacuum seal regularly, it may be worth paying more for a durable model with extra features. If you only seal food occasionally, a basic model will likely do the job. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Kara Brown is a recipe developer and beekeeper.Christine Pittman is the founder and CEO at TheCookful and CookForTwo, which provide meal-planning programs and recipes straight to your inbox. I have written about how to keep food fresh during a power outage, the best mini fridges and more. For this story, I interviewed two food experts about the benefits of vacuum sealing food. articles.title: What are Italy’s new measures against violent protests?
articles.summary: The government has unveiled a new offence of ‘violent participation in public demonstrations’, among other measures.
articles.body:
The right-wing government of Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has approved a raft of security measures , including the deployment of 500 troops in the financial capital Milan, to curb youth-led protests that turned chaotic over the weekend.

“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalising and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni wrote on social media on Tuesday, unveiling the decree.

Unrest broke out on Saturday in Milan during a peaceful rally over rising living costs and poor school conditions inspired by similar mobilisations in neighbouring Spain and France .

Groups of mainly young people looted shops, smashed windows and clashed with the police again on Sunday, with riots also reported in Bologna and Turin.

Here’s what we know about the new measures.

The Italian cabinet approved sending 500 troops to Milan until the end of the year to maintain security at key sites, step up surveillance of ‌sensitive locations, ⁠and enhance monitoring across the area, the Defence Ministry said in a statement.

It is unclear what the army will be able to do, given that the cabinet stopped short of granting soldiers additional policing powers following opposition from President Sergio Mattarella. In Italy, the army is responsible for national defence while police carry out investigations and arrest duties.

As part of the new legal measures, which take effect immediately, the government has also introduced a new offence of “violent participation in public demonstrations” targeting people gathering in groups of more than five who use potentially harmful objects including stones, sticks and fireworks.

The offence is punishable with up to five years in prison and a fine up to 20,000 euros ($22,440).

The text of the decree also cites the saying “You break it, you buy it” as grounds for making the parents of minors financially liable for the damage caused by their children. The state can claim damages for any resulting loss against parents’ properties or by deducting public subsidies received by the family.

Children and young people aged 14 to 18 will also be subject to administrative detention, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults.

Additional measures include longer prison sentences of up to 12 years for individuals who use social media or online tools to organise groups for violent public demonstrations.

Gregorio Sorgona, a historian at the University of Palermo, said the measures do not take into account growing discontent among young people, sparked by a “fundamental contradiction”: “On one hand, the ostentatiousness of wealth and richness as a model of success; on the other, a profound crisis marked by economic precariousness.”

“For the youth who live in poverty, the impossibility of accessing those symbols of wealth can spark violent behaviour and looting,” Sorgona told Al Jazeera. “Before tackling the effects, one should act on the causes, starting with growing social inequality.”

Hundreds of thousands of Europeans took to the streets in Italy, France, Spain, Belgium and Portugal on Saturday in largely uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries.

In Milan, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in the city centre, emptying Piazza del Duomo and a luxury arcade that would usually be full of shoppers.

A march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully, but masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.

Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds. At least two police officers were injured, and about 50 demonstrators – many of them minors – were detained, the Italian LaPresse news agency reported.

In Bologna, police also reported that, alongside peaceful rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers. In Turin, hooded protesters used bins and outdoor furniture to set up barricades, and threw firecrackers, sticks and stones at police.

What have the reactions to the new measures been?

Protesters say the measures fail to address the root cause of the violence, namely rising prices that are pushing families ⁠into poverty. A lack of affordable housing, rising household costs, and failing public services have led many young people to say they no longer expect to be better off than their parents.

Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average, but jumped in 2022, when annual inflation hit 8.7 percent in Italy. The surge was driven mainly by energy costs, which soared following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Between 2000 and 2025, the cost of everyday necessities such as food, energy, transport and household bills has risen by 68 percent in Italy, while the average full-time wage has fallen by almost 5 percent.

Genoa Mayor Silvia Salis said: “Young people must be listened to, but in Milan and Turin we have seen violence with the sole aim of destruction.”

“The response, however, should be inclusion,” she said, according to Italian newspaper La Repubblica.

NGOs including Associazione Antigone, which promotes human rights within the prison system, warned that arresting young people en masse will only add to pre-existing problems. More and longer prison sentences, it said, will worsen overcrowding. According to government data, the prison population in Italy has already increased by more than ⁠17 percent over four years.

The organisation said in a Facebook post that while roughly one child in seven (13.8 percent) lives in poverty, the government has not formed any policies to tackle this.

Sorgona said, therefore, that these latest measures are unlikely to prevent further protests and violence, as they failed to do in Genoa against G8 anti-globalisation demonstrators in 2001, when 300,000 protesters marched and police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets.

“Deterrence is not necessarily a valid tool to prevent the radicalisation of conflict, especially in a society that is swept by poverty and social segregation,” Sorgona said.

“The decree risks intensifying the protests and leading to the arrest of thousands of suspects on the basis of ill-defined legal grounds.”

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A special executive magistrate on Wednesday ordered the release of Cockroach Janata Party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, seven days
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A special executive magistrate on Wednesday ordered the release of Cockroach Janata Party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, seven days after they were taken into custody.The CJP leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody on October 13 following a protest at Jantar Mantar seeking CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the deletion of voters' names.CJP leaders Das and Ranka, along with 12 party members, allegedly trespassed into Jantar Mantar, which is no longer a designated protest venue, and obstructed police personnel on duty.The release order came hours after the two withdrew their petition in the Delhi high court challenging the extension of their custody.What are the conditions of releaseThe CJP leaders were released after they gave written undertakings not to breach the peace and assured the court that they would not call for any protest at Jantar Mantar as long as it remains denotified as a protest site, Live Law reported.The leaders also assured the court that any protest they organise would be conducted within the four corners of the Constitution.Read more | Watch: 'Inquilab Zindabad', CJP leaders Saurav Das & Ashutosh Ranka come out of Tihar JailIn their undertakings, Ranka and Das expressed faith in the judiciary and its institutions, including the court of the special executive magistrate. The magistrate took the undertakings on record, Live Law reported.After considering submissions from both sides and the written undertakings, the magistrate held that the immediate preventive measures under Section 135(3) of the BNSS could be secured by requiring the two leaders to execute bonds to maintain peace.Das and Ranka were also directed to furnish personal bonds and surety bonds of Rs 50,000 each until the conclusion of the inquiry.The magistrate also directed them to appear before the court on every date of hearing and maintain peace and public tranquillity in accordance with the terms of their bonds and undertakings.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Best hiking spots to try in the DFW area ahead of SMU's week eight home showdown with Cal
articles.summary: Cedar Ridge Preserve, Arbor Hills, and more hidden hiking trails near SMU Mustangs' campus make DFW a surprising fall destination for outdoors lovers.
articles.body: As we ascend deeper and deeper into the college football season, the hiking becomes more and more about finding places that aren't frigid. If you're looking for a locale that offers comfortable fall temperatures without having to pack a parka, might I suggest the Dallas-Ft. Worth area? It just so happens the 23rd-ranked SMU Mustangs are hosting the Cal Golden Bears this Saturday, and their stadium, located in the scenic Highland Park neighborhood of Dallas, is within driving distance of a ton of great trails. FSU-SMU GAME TURNS INTO OLD-SCHOOL FOOTBALL AFTER STADIUM POWER OUTAGE WIPES OUT IN-GAME COMMUNICATION Most people likely think of DFW as nothing but a vast sea of highways and high rises, but having been a resident of the Metroplex for six years, I can attest that there are plenty of beautiful hikes just waiting to be found. Get to know some of these hidden gems as you make your way to North Texas for the game this weekend. BEST HIKES TO TRY AROUND LUBBOCK AHEAD OF TEXAS TECH'S WEEK ONE MATCHUP WITH ABILENE CHRISTIAN 1. Cedar Ridge Preserve As I mentioned, you might think DFW is just some sprawling urban nightmare with nothing but flat terrain, but our top choice on this list debunks that misconception right from the jump. Cedar Ridge Preserve is located roughly 15 miles southwest of downtown Dallas and features nearly nine miles of hilly trails and scenic overlooks thanks to being nearly 800 feet above sea level. The wooded hiking trails will make you feel like you are hundreds of miles away from civilization despite being just a stone's throw from one of the most populous cities in America; the best of both worlds! If you want a taste of Texas Hill Country without ever having to leave the DFW Metroplex, put Cedar Ridge Preserve on your list. 2. Arbor Hills Nature Preserve I might be a little biased on this one since it's where I had one of my first dates with my now-wife and was the site of our engagement photos, but Arbor Hills Nature Preserve is a must-see for anyone visiting Dallas during the fall. Located in the nearby suburb of Plano, Arbor Hills is a straight shot up the Dallas North Tollway and is a bit more central in terms of location than Cedar Ridge, but this place really has it all. Both paved and unpaved trails are offered here as well as a bike path for anyone looking to explore on two wheels. A special mention has to be made to the observation tower at the center of the park, which features a great view of the fall foliage of North Texas. Make your way to the top of the tower at sunset and the scenes from up there will surely be Instagram-worthy. Arbor Hills has wooded paths, open prairies, and even a creek, presenting the whole package to any outdoorsman without ever leaving the confines of the city. 3. Fort Worth Nature Center and Refuge Don't forget, there is an "FW" in the "DFW" area, and Fort Worth might be an even better hiking city than its more famous sister. For those of you interested in a more western flavor to your trip, Fort Worth is the place to be, and the Fort Worth Nature Center and Refuge is the gold standard of Tarrant County trails. NATIONAL PARK SERVICE DIRECTOR CALLS YELLOWSTONE'S WILD BISON RECOVERY AN 'INCREDIBLE CONSERVATION STORY' The Refuge is super distinctive in its looks, with tree-covered trails and wetlands that connect to both the Trinity River and Lake Worth. This place has everything from a boardwalks to natural paths and there are even bison on the property. It's a bit of a trek from SMU's campus, but if you're in DFW for the whole weekend, I would recommend giving it a look and then enjoying some of the excellent barbecue in the area to refuel. 4. Oak Cliff Nature Preserve The final entry on our list is a bit of a local hidden gem, but it shouldn't be too hard to find. Nestled just to the southwest of downtown Dallas, Oak Cliff Nature Preserve is a 121-acre sanctuary with thick, overgrown vegetation and dirt paths to remind you that there is still plenty of natural beauty in this overgrown concrete jungle. There is one interconnected single track that takes you around the property, but it stretches nearly eight miles, so those of you looking to hit your step goal will be in heaven. Bikers are welcome, too, as the nature preserve is very popular with mountain bike enthusiasts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Anyone looking for a no-frills alternative to walking around the downtown area should definitely give this place a hard look, and history buffs will be happy, as the Oak Cliff Nature Preserve is just a short drive from the Texas Theater, where alleged JFK assassin Lee Harvey Oswald snuck into a movie while on the run from Dallas police.

articles.title: San Francisco's Freedom West co-op was created after 1960s urban renewal displaced Black families; a new $23 million boost could unlock a 2,400-home rebuild while keeping longtime residents as owners
articles.summary: A housing cooperative established to help Black and immigrant families remain in San Francisco after urban renewal displaced residents from the historic
articles.body: A housing cooperative established to help Black and immigrant families remain in San Francisco after urban renewal displaced residents from the historic Fillmore neighbourhood is moving closer to a major redevelopment. Freedom West Homes has secured a $23 million city subsidy, alongside private financing, for its long-planned transformation into a residential district with nearly 2,400 homes. According to the San Francisco Chronicle and local news outlet SFist, the project is designed to replace ageing buildings while allowing longtime cooperative shareholders to retain their ownership stakes rather than being pushed out by redevelopment.The proposed redevelopment, known as Freedom West 2.0, covers a 10-acre site in San Francisco’s Western Addition. The revised plan calls for nearly 2,400 homes, of which 17% would be income-restricted. It also includes a new affordable senior housing building intended to accommodate current residents as the larger project advances in phases. The funding boost marks an important step for a project that has faced financial challenges because of its unusual cooperative ownership structure and the cost of replacing ageing housing.A cooperative born out of displacementFreedom West’s origins are closely linked to the urban renewal programmes that reshaped San Francisco’s Fillmore District during the mid-20th century. The neighbourhood had developed into an important centre of African American life, culture and business, particularly as Black residents moved to San Francisco during the Great Migration. Redevelopment projects later cleared large areas of the Western Addition, displacing residents and disrupting established communities and businesses.Freedom West was among the housing initiatives that emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s in response to that upheaval. The cooperative was created to give Black and immigrant families a way to remain in the neighbourhood through shared ownership rather than relying solely on rental housing. Its complex was completed in 1973 and consists of 382 cooperative homes spread across four blocks, according to SFist.The cooperative’s land is bounded by Gough Street, Fulton Street, Golden Gate Avenue and Laguna Street, surrounding the historically African American Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church. The site is home to around 1,000 cooperative shareholders, about half of whom are senior citizens. Many have family connections to the original development and view ownership as a way to preserve a foothold in a neighbourhood transformed by decades of redevelopment and rising housing costs.The cooperative model is central to the project’s purpose. Rather than simply replacing older buildings with new apartments, Freedom West 2.0 aims to preserve the residents’ ownership interests while creating additional housing on the site. Freedom West’s board president, Mattie Scott, said the founders created the cooperative so that Black and immigrant families displaced from the Fillmore could continue to live in the area and own homes there. The redevelopment, she said, should allow those families to remain part of the neighbourhood’s future.How the 2,400-home plan will workThe current proposal is smaller than an earlier version of the redevelopment plan, which envisioned 2,515 homes. The revised scheme combines replacement cooperative housing with market-rate development and affordable homes, allowing the organisation to use the value of part of its land to help finance the rebuilding of the existing complex.Under the plan described by SFist, Freedom West intends to sell roughly two-thirds of its property to market-rate developers and redevelop the remaining third for affordable housing and replacement cooperative homes. The proposed mix includes 1,885 market-rate homes and 267 replacement co-op units, alongside the initial senior housing phase. Overall, 17% of the planned homes would be income-restricted.The first stage, known as Phase 0, is planned as a 115-unit affordable housing building for seniors at 880 McAllister Street. It is intended to provide housing for older residents as the wider redevelopment moves forward. SFist reported that Freedom West was targeting a groundbreaking in mid-2027 for this initial phase. That is a planned milestone, not confirmation that construction has begun.The broader project also involves a proposed 25-year development agreement with San Francisco. According to the San Francisco Chronicle, the agreement would provide long-term planning certainty and allow zoning for buildings of up to 345 feet on the site. The city’s financial support and private gap financing are intended to help bridge the difference between the cost of development and the funds available through conventional housing programmes.Why funding has been difficultFinancing Freedom West 2.0 has presented a challenge because the property operates as a limited-equity cooperative rather than a conventional affordable rental development. Many established affordable housing subsidies and tax-credit programmes are designed around rental properties, making them difficult to apply to a project in which residents own shares in a cooperative.To help address this issue, the redevelopment's financing strategy includes private contributions and a mechanism that would use future property tax revenues to support affordable housing. The San Francisco Chronicle reported that the new $23 million city subsidy, combined with private financing from organisations including the Crankstart Foundation, provides important financial momentum.The latest funding announcement follows earlier efforts to raise money for the project. In December 2024, Freedom West announced that commitments from organisations including the San Francisco Foundation, Low Income Investment Fund and Menorah Park had brought its predevelopment funding to more than $30 million. The organisation described the wider Freedom West 2.0 plan as a $2.3 billion revitalisation project.That earlier fundraising was intended to support the work needed before construction, including planning and development. It should not be confused with the total construction budget or the newly announced $23 million subsidy.Redevelopment without losing ownershipFor Freedom West, the challenge is to modernise an ageing complex without repeating the displacement that led to its creation. Its cooperative structure gives residents a stake in the property, and the redevelopment plan is intended to preserve that stake through replacement homes. The organisation has said it wants current shareholders to move into modernised housing without additional monthly housing costs.The proposal also reflects a wider dilemma for historically Black neighbourhoods: how to replace deteriorating housing and add homes without excluding the people who have maintained communities there for generations. New construction can expand the housing supply, but its benefits depend in part on who can afford to remain and who has a say in shaping the neighbourhood.Freedom West 2.0 is not yet a completed redevelopment, and its construction will unfold over multiple phases. But the new financial support moves the proposal forward while keeping resident ownership at its centre. articles.title: Minnesota tribal leaders have cut a proposed casino land-trust request from roughly 300 acres to 80 after local concerns, but the site still needs federal approval and the governor’s concurrence
articles.summary: A Native American tribe planning to build a casino in Minnesota has reduced its land request from nearly 300 acres to 80 acres after local officials
articles.body: A Native American tribe planning to build a casino in Minnesota has reduced its land request from nearly 300 acres to 80 acres after local officials raised concerns about drinking water, traffic and taxes. The White Earth Nation had initially planned to seek federal trust status for approximately 297 acres in Clay County. However, the tribe has now decided to seek approval for a much smaller area. The casino still needs federal approval and the agreement of Minnesota's governor before the project can move forward.The decision was discussed at a meeting between tribal representatives and Clay County commissioners on October 13. Local officials wanted to know how the proposed casino would affect nearby communities, including whether it would increase traffic, put pressure on public services or reduce local tax revenue.The proposed site is in Glyndon Township, near Highway 336 and County Road 74. According to Tribal Business News and The Flag, the tribe has already carried out studies to examine whether a casino would be practical at the location. However, questions remain about the final building plans, road access, and possible effects on the environment. The tribe has not yet submitted its application to the federal government.Why are local officials worried ?One of the main concerns is the possible effect on the Buffalo Aquifer, an underground source of water that supplies drinking water to Moorhead residents.During the meeting, Commissioner Campbell questioned whether construction and other activities at the site could affect this water supply. He asked for more information about the studies conducted on the land before the county considers supporting the project.Officials are also worried about traffic. A casino could bring more vehicles onto Highway 336 and County Road 74, raising questions about whether the existing roads would be able to handle them.Commissioners said the area might need major road improvements. The tribe acknowledged that more studies and discussions would be needed to understand the possible costs.Taxes are another concern. The tribe wants the federal government to hold the land in trust on its behalf. If approved, the land would no longer be subject to ordinary local property taxes.This has raised questions about how the county would pay for public services connected to the development. Officials want to know whether the casino would create additional costs for roads, water supply, emergency services and other facilities.Why did the tribe reduce its land request?Nate Matthews, special projects manager for the tribe, explained that the smaller proposal was intended to address concerns about placing such a large area under federal trust.He also said the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the federal agency involved in the process, had recommended seeking approval only for land needed for the casino and possible future expansion.The tribe has shared an early plan showing a casino, parking spaces, a possible campground and areas for other businesses.However, commissioners questioned why the tribe needed 80 acres when an earlier drawing appeared to show a smaller development.Matthews explained that the design was not final and could change. The tribe has also not decided exactly how the 80 acres would be arranged. The smaller land request therefore does not mean that all concerns have been resolved.Casino could take until 2028 to receive approvalBefore the casino can be built, the tribe must complete a federal approval process known as a two-part secretarial determination.Under this process, federal authorities must approve the proposal, and Minnesota's governor must also agree. The tribe cannot begin building a casino on the land simply because it has reduced the size of its request.Jacob Severson, who handles land purchases and trust applications for the tribe, explained that the process involves several stages.Once the application is submitted, federal officials have 120 days to check whether all the required documents have been provided.The government would then carry out further reviews, including examining the possible environmental effects and consulting local authorities.The full process could take between 18 and 36 months, depending on how much additional information is needed."So, the best case, absolute best case scenario would be 2028 sometime, likely towards the end of 2028," Severson told commissioners.What happens next?The White Earth Nation has already completed several studies, including an assessment of whether the casino could be financially successful. It has also examined soil conditions and carried out preliminary environmental work.The next steps include sharing information about underground water with Moorhead Public Service and continuing studies on traffic, roads, water and sewer connections.The tribe has also suggested forming a group with representatives from Clay County, Moorhead and other local authorities. The aim would be to discuss how the casino could affect public services and who would pay for any additional costs.One possibility being discussed is that the tribe could make payments to local governments to help cover services, even though land held in federal trust would not be subject to ordinary property taxes.White Earth Nation Chairman Michael Fairbanks has said the casino project is intended to create jobs, support healthcare and bring investment to the region."Economic development not only brings jobs and healthcare, it strengthens the whole area," Fairbanks told commissioners.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘The American dream is not for sale’: Feds bust Mass. marriage fraud ring
articles.summary: Federal authorities announced Wednesday that they have broken up an alleged marriage fraud ring that arranged hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts designed to obtain unlawful immigration benefits.
articles.body: Federal authorities announced Wednesday that they have broken up an alleged marriage fraud ring that arranged hundreds of sham marriages in Massachusetts designed to obtain unlawful immigration benefits. U.S. Attorney Leah Foley was joined by Homeland Security and immigration officials at a press conference at the Moakley courthouse on Wednesday morning to detail charges against six people, five of whom they said are currently in federal custody. Foley said the marriage fraud ring generated over $6 million in profit and spanned more than a decade. The ringleader was Fall River resident Jennifer Gonzalez, a U.S. citizen who arranged the marriages, charging between $38,000-$40,000 and arranging between 18-20 marriages a year. Gonzalez then used the money to invest in businesses and property in the Dominican Republic. “Every time I have a spare dollar I just invest in new property in my country,” she allegedly said. “Like, I have a lot of land in my country.” Gonzalez also secured payments for her co-conspirators, who were paid to engage in one or more fake marriages so that people could obtain U.S. citizenship and submit fraudulent documents. According to court documents, the others charged were Erica Daniels, Cherice Alejandro, Amara Pugh, Jessica Tavares and Jaylin Hill, all of Fall River. Foley said Gonzalez ran “a very sophisticated operation” that could have gone on for much longer, if it weren’t for someone coming forward to tip off federal authorities. She said court filings show that Gonzalez was caught on video explaining the process of participating in the sham marriages, which included taking the couples’ photos to make the relationships seem real. In those recordings, she also explained how her business became more challenging when Donald Trump became president in 2024, and said she suspended her business in 2025 because immigration “was a little harsh.” Gonzalez has a prior criminal history, Foley said, including convictions for assault and battery, identity fraud and fraud, illegal entry, possession of burglars tools and knowingly receiving stolen property. She also allegedly entered a fraudulent marriage herself to get the other person illegal benefits. The others involved also had criminal histories, including assault, weapons and drug charges and affiliations with know street gangs. Foley said Gonzalez also applied for and received approximately $124,500 in SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts between 2019 and 2026. “It is alleged Ms. Gonzalez got rich by selling the American dream, all the while by sending money to another country,” Foley said. “The American dream is not for sale. It is earned. And when you try to pilfer it for profit, we will hold you accountable.” Federal authorities said their investigation is ongoing.

articles.title: Randy Houser opens up about his lifelong love of fishing and unforgettable trip with Navy SEALs
articles.summary: From fishing in Mississippi to unforgettable days on the water with Navy SEALs, Randy Houser shares why the outdoors will always be part of his life.
articles.body: Country music star Randy Houser spends a lot of his life on the road, but when the shows are over and the tour bus stops rolling, there's usually one thing on his mind. Finding somewhere to fish. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS "When I get off the tour bus, I'm literally looking for some water to get on," Houser told OutKick OutDoors in an exclusive interview. For the Mississippi native, that love of fishing started long before the hit songs, sold-out shows and life on the road. "Growing up in Mississippi, that's about all we had. We had bluegill, catfish and bass," he said. These days, Houser's fishing adventures have taken him a little farther from home. He's traded the freshwater lakes of Mississippi for the turquoise waters of the Bahamas, where he's developed a particular fondness for fly fishing. "I spend a lot of time bonefishing in the Bahamas. That's kind of my thing now, as I enjoy fly fishing for bonefish and permit and things like that," he explained. "I spend a lot of my time doing that in the winter." And while getting away from the demands of touring is certainly part of the appeal, Houser's connection to the water runs deeper than simply needing a vacation. "I think that stems from all the time I spent on the water as a kid," he said. It's also a passion he shares with his wife and children, who frequently join him on the water. But one of Houser's most memorable fishing experiences wasn't about the size of the fish or the destination. It was about the people he shared it with. More than just fishing The country star recalled a three-day bonefishing trip to Blackfly Lodge in the Bahamas with the Navy SEAL Foundation, where he spent time alongside active and retired Navy SEALs. "I'm a huge supporter of our military and military families and personnel," Houser said. "To get that time with those guys and get them in a space where they're on the water and can relax, and just to hear stories that they wouldn't normally talk about in a different situation, was just priceless." For Houser, the opportunity to connect with those men away from their everyday responsibilities made the trip unforgettable. "I got to hear just personal experiences from those guys," he said. "I'll remember it forever. It was really cool." Now, Houser is preparing to bring his love of music and fishing together in a big way. Country music meets bass fishing in Nashville On Friday, Oct. 30, he'll perform alongside his friend and fellow country star Riley Green at The Pinnacle in Nashville as part of The Champions, a new professional bass fishing tournament hosted by World Bass Enterprises. The tournament, held on Old Hickory Lake, brings together top anglers from the Bassmaster Elite Series and Major League Fishing's Bass Pro Tour to compete for a record $3.25 million purse, including $1.25 million for the winner. For someone who grew up fishing for fun in Mississippi, Houser said it's remarkable to see just how far competitive bass fishing has come. He recalled learning that a friend's son was competing on a college bass fishing team and thinking about how different things were when he was growing up. "I thought, wow, what a dream," he said. "If I was in high school, I'd have been thinking, 'Lord, you mean I can get a scholarship to go fishing?'" SUPERMOTOCROSS CHAMPION LEVI KITCHEN WANTS TO TRY TOURNAMENT BASS FISHING WHEN HE HANGS UP HIS HELMET Houser compared the difficulty of becoming a successful professional angler to making it as a professional golfer, noting the tremendous skill, sponsorships and resources necessary to compete at the highest level. And he believes Nashville is the perfect place to showcase how much the sport has grown. "There's a strong synergy between country music, country music listeners and bass fishing," he said. With Old Hickory and Percy Priest lakes nearby, Houser is familiar with the area's fishing opportunities. He's spent plenty of time fishing Old Hickory himself and expects The Champions to draw a significant crowd, both for the concerts and the competition. "I think they're going to have a lot more fans than they expected," he said. "Not just for the music at The Pinnacle, but also hanging out at the lake waiting for the weigh-ins and things like that." Houser is especially looking forward to performing with Green, whom he considers a good friend. The two have spent plenty of time touring together, although their busy schedules haven't allowed for much fishing lately. They do, however, have plans to do some hunting together once the weather cools down. Another bonus of The Champions taking place in Nashville? Houser gets to bring his children to the show — something he said doesn't happen very often. For a man who grew up with a fishing rod in his hands, it's a fitting opportunity to celebrate just how far the sport has come while sharing the experience with his own family. articles.title: Tribute paid to Bridgend woman who died of 'stab wounds' after crash
articles.summary: It is understood Eleanor Barnfield, from Bridgend, had been stabbed before the crash.
articles.body:
Tributes have been paid to a woman who crashed a car into a wall after allegedly being stabbed.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing.

A 61-year-old man from Bridgend has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a "significant" police operation at a retirement housing complex, and remains in custody.

Eleanor, who worked for housing association Valleys to Coast which runs the complex, has been described by her family as the "kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world".

South Wales Police said Eleanor was taken to hospital after officers were called to the crash on Coity Road at about 12:40 BST on Monday, but later died.

Police were also called to nearby sheltered housing retirement complex, Ger-y-Nant, where the man was arrested.

Describing Eleanor, from North Cornelly, Bridgend, her family said: "She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock."

Jo Oak, chief executive of Valleys to Coast, added the organisation was "devastated by the tragic death of our colleague".

"Eleanor was a much-valued member of the Valleys to Coast team, and her loss has been deeply felt by everyone who knew and worked alongside her," she said.

"She made an important contribution to our organisation and to the communities we serve, and she will be remembered with great warmth and affection by her colleagues.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with Eleanor's family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time."

Oak said the organisation would "continue to cooperate fully with South Wales Police".

Ch Supt Jason Rees said: "Our thoughts remain firmly with Eleanor's family. I want to assure the community that teams of detectives and specialist staff are investigating.

"We appreciate the patience and support of residents, especially those displaced following the incident. Local communities may notice an increased police presence as our investigation continues."

articles.title: Bray: Investigation after man and woman found dead
articles.summary: The bodies of a man in his 30s and a woman in her 40s are discovered at the same house in Bray.
articles.body:
Gardaí (Irish police) are investigating after a woman in her 40s and a man in his 30s were found dead at a house in Bray, County Dublin.

Their bodies were discovered at the property in Cois Cairn, on Old Connaught Avenue, shortly after 08:00 local time on Wednesday.

They have been named locally as couple Bridgid 'Biddy' O'Brien and James McGinn, according to Irish broadcaster RTÉ.

In a statement, gardaí said the outcome of post-mortem examinations would assist in determining the course of the investigation.

The examinations will be carried out by state pathologist over the course of Wednesday and Thursday.

A cordon was put in place in the housing estate on Wednesday morning and a large blue forensic tent was erected at the scene.

A senior officer has been appointed to lead the investigation from an incident room at Dún Laoghaire Garda Station, with support from the Serious Crime Unit.

Family liaison officers are supporting relatives of the deceased.

Councillor Malachaí Duddy, Cathaoirleach (Chair) of Bray Municipal District, said the whole community was shocked by the deaths.

"It's a very sad day and it's a tragedy," he told BBC News NI.

"I extend my condolences to the family."

Duddy added that Bray is famed for its sense of community and he had no doubt that local residents would pull together in difficult times.

He urged the public to cooperate with the gardaí and to contact them if they had any information about the deaths.

articles.title: Macron makes surprise Saudi visit as France secures extra diesel supplies
articles.summary: French president meets Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh to discuss energy, security, and infrastructure.
articles.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron has arrived in Riyadh on a surprise “solidarity” visit, making him the first Western leader to touch down in Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s Houthis intensified their attacks this month.

Macron met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Saudi capital, and the two discussed regional and international developments, as well as coordinating efforts to strengthen security and stability, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported on Wednesday.

The unannounced trip comes as Saudi Arabia agreed to supply extra diesel to France “for as many months as necessary”, the Elysee Palace told the AFP news agency.

The visit aims to “demonstrate France’s solidarity with the kingdom in the face of the attacks carried out by the Houthis against its territory, and to continue efforts undertaken on securing and diversifying hydrocarbon supplies”, the French presidency said earlier.

The diplomatic push follows days of rioting in France, fuelled by the cost of living, especially as the US-Iran war and Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have kept energy prices high.

Faced with criticism of his Gulf tour at home, Macron told reporters earlier in Doha that he was just “doing his job” in a bid to “ease tensions” over petrol prices, one of the causes of social unrest in France.

“There must be no sign of febrility,” he said. “I am fulfilling my role. I am at my post.”

The deal follows pledges secured earlier in Macron’s Gulf tour. The presidency said on Tuesday that the United Arab Emirates had committed to about 100,000 tonnes a month , with a further 100,000 tonnes monthly to be secured in Bahrain.

Together with Saudi deliveries, France now has commitments for 295,000 tonnes a month, just more than 10 percent of its consumption, it said.

Meanwhile, France is also sending military assets to Saudi Arabia , under an earlier agreement, to help protect the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has come under attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

The United Kingdom also announced on Tuesday that it would deploy fighter jets to help shield the kingdom. Both countries say their support is purely defensive.

Analysts say the moves protect Saudi oil exports that matter to Europe’s energy markets and bolster the Gulf alliance as the US shows reluctance to offer direct military help. They also carry risks, analysts say, potentially drawing the two European states into the protracted Saudi-Houthi conflict.

articles.title: Tennessee Titans cut DL Jordan Elliott after he allegedly brought a gun to team facility
articles.summary: The Tennessee Titans cut defensive lineman Jordan Elliott after he brought a gun to the team’s training facility in a “terrible lapse of judgement,” officials said Wednesday.
articles.body: The Tennessee Titans cut defensive lineman Jordan Elliott after he brought a gun to the team’s training facility in a “terrible lapse of judgement,” officials said Wednesday. Titans coach Robert Saleh defended Elliott and called his now-former player “a good man” who deserves another chance — but just not in Tennessee. “He’s a good man (who) had a terrible lapse in judgment that I recognize as a call for help more than a than a criminal act,” Saleh told reporters. “It’s unfortunate the way it went down.” Union officials and Elliott’s agent could not be immediately reached for comment on Wednesday. It wasn’t immediately clear what might have prompted Elliott to bring a firearm to the team’s Nashville headquarters. Nashville police were not called and did not respond to the scene, the department said Wednesday. “The league’s firearm policy prohibits any personnel from bringing a firearm to club facilities, stadiums, and team hotels and on team planes or buses,” the NFL said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday. “The club promptly notified the league of the matter which is under review.” Elliott had played in Tennessee’s first five games this season before being listed as inactive on Sunday for “not injury related, personal” reasons. Then by Tuesday, he was off the team. “On Thursday, October 15, there was an incident at our team facility involving Jordan Elliott,” according to a Titans statement. “Following our review of the incident, we have made the decision to release Elliott from our roster. We will have no further comment on the matter.” Elliott signed with Tennessee this past off season, following two years with the San Francisco 49ers and then four previous campaigns with the Cleveland Browns. Elliott’s move to Nashville made for a reunion between he and Titans first-year coach Saleh, who was the defensive coordinator in Santa Clara last season. The coach said he hopes Elliott can sign with another team and that he’d vouch for the player’s character. “Unfortunately rules are rules with regards to guns on (team) property,” Saleh said. “My message to 31 other teams would be: If you need a hell of a run-stopping D tackle that can help you on a playoff run, give me a call. I’ll tell you everything you need to know about him.” The 28-year-old Houston native played college football for the Texas Longhorns and Missouri Tigers before he was taken by Cleveland in the third round of the 2020 NFL Draft. “At the end of the day, we’re all humans,” QB Cam Ward said. “We’re all with him. I mean he’s a great person.”

articles.summary: When wildfires tore through Maui in August 2023, the damage extended well beyond the buildings reduced to ash.
articles.body: When wildfires tore through Maui in August 2023, the damage extended well beyond the buildings reduced to ash. Families lost their homes, neighbourhoods were disrupted and the shortage of affordable housing became harder to manage. For residents already struggling with the cost of living on the Hawaiian island, finding somewhere to live became an additional concern. As reported by Maui Now, in October 2024, Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sanchez donated $3 million to Habitat for Humanity Maui, providing support for affordable housing programmes and work to repair and rebuild homes affected by the fires.Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sanchez's $3 million donation to Habitat for Humanity MauiHabitat for Humanity Maui announced the contribution on 29 October 2024. The gift was among the largest the organisation had received in its history, according to the announcement, and came as the island continued to deal with the consequences of the wildfires and an existing shortage of affordable homes.The funding was intended to help the organisation expand its housing work, including construction and repair projects for local families. Some of the money would go towards rebuilding homes damaged by the fires, while other support would help more residents access homeownership.The donation also gave the organisation additional resources to increase its building capacity. For a community facing substantial housing needs, the ability to undertake more projects can affect how many families receive assistance and how quickly homes can be repaired or built.Maui wildfires increased the need for affordable housing and home repairsThe wildfires that struck Maui in August 2023 caused widespread destruction, particularly in the historic town of Lahaina. Homes and businesses were lost, and many residents had to leave areas where they had lived for years. The disaster placed further pressure on an island where housing costs were already a persistent concern.Recovery involved more than clearing damaged sites and replacing buildings. Residents also needed access to housing they could afford while rebuilding plans moved forward. For households on lower incomes, returning to the island or remaining close to their communities could be difficult when available accommodation was limited and expensive.Habitat for Humanity Maui's work covered both the construction of homes and the repair of existing properties. The Bezos and Sanchez contribution was intended to strengthen those efforts, helping the organisation respond to the needs of families whose housing circumstances had been affected by the fires.How Habitat for Humanity Maui supports local familiesAs reported, Habitat for Humanity Maui has worked on affordable housing on the island for more than 25 years. Its programmes are designed to help households who might struggle to secure suitable housing through the conventional market.The organisation builds and repairs homes for qualifying families using a model that does not charge interest or generate a profit on the housing provided. According to its published description, it serves households earning between 25% and 80% of Maui County's median income.The October 2024 donation was intended to support this existing work while allowing the organisation to reach more households. It was not limited to a single rebuilding project, with the stated uses also covering wider affordable housing programmes and access to homeownership.The role of private giving in the recovery effortThe contribution formed part of a wider effort to address Maui's housing needs following the fires. Local organisations, public agencies and private donors have all had roles in the island's recovery, although the scale of demand has meant that housing remains a long-term concern rather than a problem that can be resolved through one funding announcement.For Habitat for Humanity Maui, the $3 million gift offered additional resources for its construction and repair work. articles.title: Ohio governor's race turns ugly as attack ad features candidate's estranged mother
articles.summary: The Republican candidate released an ad featuring his opponent's mother calling her daughter "a liar".
articles.body:
The race to be Ohio's next governor has turned ugly amid uproar over one of the most viral attack ads of the midterm elections campaign.

Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy released an ad featuring his opponent's estranged mother urging Ohioans not to elect her daughter.

"She's lied her entire life," Donna Arthur says in the video.

But the ad leaves out that her daughter, Democratic candidate Amy Acton, alleged she was raped by Arthur's husband 40 years ago when she was just 12.

Acton's brother said turning alleged sexual assault into "a political talking point" was a "despicable low". Experts told the BBC that the jarringly personal nature of the political attack will likely backfire.

Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged in 1978.

That's when she last spoke to her mother, Acton said in an interview with The Vindicator, an Ohio news outlet. The Arthurs fled Ohio, and he was never prosecuted on the rape charge. He died in 2004.

Political attacks ads are not a new feature of US politics, but they have grown more coarse, experts say.

"They have become more intense, and the boundaries have stretched in terms of what one attacks about," said David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs.

Lublin also said it was not new for relatives to be used against a political opponent, mentioning family members who testified against Robert F Kennedy Jr before he was confirmed as health secretary.

"But this is of a different order," Lublin said. "They're estranged not over policy but over a rape allegation."

The BBC has reached out to Ramaswamy's campaign for comment. In a statement to the BBC's US partner, CBS News, a campaign spokesman reiterated assertions in the ad that Acton was untruthful, but conceded, "We don't know what happened between Amy and her mother".

When the ad was initially released to social media on Monday evening, it did not say who the video was paid for or authorised by. But Ramaswamy confirmed on Tuesday that it came from his campaign, and he later pledged to spend $4m (£2.9m) to further air it.

The move drew intense backlash from Democrats.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said on X it was "an abhorrent attack". Illinois governor and 2028 presidential hopeful JB Pritzker said Ramaswamy "has reached a new low by launching these vile and false attacks".

Acton's team released its own campaign ad on Tuesday, a video featuring her brother, Philip Stearns, recounting childhood abuse and saying "Amy always got the worst of it".

"Shame on Vivek," he says in the 30-second clip. "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio."

Some Republicans also criticised the ad. Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for president in 2024, said "he's a bad guy. It's a shame he continues to get away with it".

Vice-President JD Vance, when asked by the BBC if he thought the ad was appropriate, did not say. "It's not really my concern," he said. "What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government."

Lublin said President Donald Trump's rhetoric and campaigns have helped act as a catalyst for the coarsening of American political discourse - he mentioned when Trump appeared to mock a reporter in Ohio who had a disability.

"We live in an age where certainly many candidates can appear mean and even inappropriate at times," Lublin said.

"The key purpose of attack ads isn't necessarily to convert the followers of your opponent, but more to depress their turnout," he said.

But Lublin expects the Ramaswamy attack ad to backfire. He said it could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favor in the increasingly competitive race for Ohio governor - even though a Democrat has not been elected governor there in over two decades.

Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has moved the Ohio governor's race from "leans Republican" to "toss up".

articles.title: Where Trump sees a deal, Putin sees a win for Russia
articles.summary: If only Donald Trump were President of Russia, he would surely agree a quick and easy deal to end the brutal Ukraine war, even – he might suggest – in as little as 24 hours.
articles.body: If only Donald Trump were President of Russia, he would surely agree a quick and easy deal to end the brutal Ukraine war, even – he might suggest – in as little as 24 hours. It is, from Trump’s point of view, a no-brainer. Not only would a resolution to the grinding conflict, now in its fifth year, halt the killing of what Trump refers to as the thousands of “young, beautiful kids” being slaughtered every month on the front lines, but it would – crucially – also be immensely profitable. Sanctions on Moscow could be swept away while lucrative trade deals would inevitably ensue. Peace and prosperity, in other words, would prevail. But, of course, Trump is not the President of Russia. That would be President Vladimir Putin, and the actual Kremlin strongman appears to have very little interest in compromising his stated war aims in Ukraine, either for the sake of Russian and Ukrainian lives or even for billions of dollars more in his state coffers. It is a fundamental misunderstanding that has driven the Trump administration’s fruitless efforts to broker an end to the fighting, and which was again on show during the latest critical meeting in St. Petersburg between Trump’s business buddy-turned-top negotiator, Steve Witkoff, and Putin himself. At the table, Putin told Witkoff he was “curious” about the outcome of meetings in Norway the day before, where officials from the US, Europe and NATO huddled with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine to hammer out new potential peace proposals, including economic incentives for Moscow. Later, a top Kremlin aide confirmed Trump’s envoy briefed the Russian leader on the discussions, before adding, inevitably, that “in truth, these contained little of actual value for resolving the Ukrainian crisis.” It was an entirely predictable outcome from a Kremlin that has stubbornly refused to budge from its hardline positions, including gaining control over the entire Donbas region of eastern Ukraine and a say in Kyiv’s future security arrangements. Still, the White House may have genuinely hoped the Kremlin would show more willingness to compromise, especially after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports last week – a politically-driven bid to ease fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, but also a huge economic boon for Moscow. Later, Trump announced an (unsuccessful) energy ceasefire that would have compelled Ukraine to halt damaging drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Amid the recriminations, during which US intelligence sharing was impacted, Trump also called for a change in the Ukrainian leadership – all music to the Kremlin’s ears. For Moscow, though, the deals, the incentives, and even the shared disdain for Kyiv are not seen as a cue to play ball and back down, but as a sign that its US strategy is yielding results. And that strategy, unlike Washington’s, is clear-eyed, with the Kremlin leader understanding what motivates Trump and effortlessly distracting his temperamental opposite number in the White House with the promise of vast economic deals. More of those were tabled by the Kremlin at the Witkoff meeting in St. Petersburg, where Putin praised the controversial diesel deal before suggesting Russia could also step up exports of crucial fertilizers to the US, and much more. “We are also discussing different projects such as data centers, projects in energy and energy cooperation,” Kiril Dmitriev, the head of the Russian sovereign wealth fund and a key Kremlin interlocutor with Trump administration officials, said after the three-hour-long talks broke up. And it’s not just economic baubles that the Kremlin uses to flatter and charm, or to keep a sympathetic ear at the White House. Putin’s release – ahead of the St. Petersburg meeting – of a 74-year-old US citizen, Stephen Hubbard, held by Russia since being captured in Ukraine in 2022, at the start of Moscow’s full-scale invasion, was cast by a fawning Witkoff as the act of “a humanitarian.” Hubbard, originally from Michigan, is reported to have suffered acute health problems during his four long years of captivity in a remote Russian penal colony. But his eventual release was lauded by the White House as a sign of Trump’s deal-making prowess and Putin’s deference. “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia,” read a statement posted on Trump’s own Truth Social platform. But it’s unlikely the tough former KGB officer in the Kremlin sees it that way.

Gonzalez also allegedly said her goal was to give all her children pieces of land in the Dominican Republic they could later own.
