articles.title: Why social media has become an election issue in Brazil’s presidential race
articles.summary: Critics have accused the tech giant Meta of censoring the political campaign of President Lula and favouring Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
In the race to be Brazil’s next president, the final two candidates are appealing to voters not only at rallies but online as well.

On Sunday, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva will face right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the final round of the election.

The race is expected to be tight. But in its final days, questions have festered over whether the digital arena has been a level playing field for the two candidates.

The social media giant Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, has faced accusations before Brazil’s top election authority, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), that it suppressed Lula’s content and favoured material promoting Bolsonaro.

Meta’s products rank among the most popular social media platforms in Brazil, and political ad spending on its sites has grown at a breakneck pace.

An analysis from the Brazilian news outlet G1 found that Meta received at least 288m Brazilian reais ($57m) in direct campaign spending in 2026, double what it received during the 2022 presidential race.

That increase marks a shift in how Brazil runs elections. More than 76 percent of Brazilian voters now get their news online, said Andre K Rodarte, a researcher at the Digital Democracy Centre at the University of Southern Denmark.

With social media eclipsing traditional advertising, Rodarte explained that a growing class of politicians is using provocative, viral messaging to connect with voters.

He pointed to the success of online influencers like right-wing personality Nikolas Ferreira and left-wing activist Erika Hilton, who each were reelected this year to Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies with record numbers of votes.

“You are seeing people transitioning from information-producer roles to politics, and they are just getting more and more power, more and more votes,” Rodarte told Al Jazeera. “If this is the media landscape they are dealing with, it’s unlikely they will adopt a different campaign style, or different style of politics.”

But critics warn that this shift to online campaigning has put political hopefuls at the mercy of Big Tech corporations and their biases.

In Brazil, the reliance on online campaigning first took off in 2018, with the election of President Jair Bolsonaro, according to Leticia Cesarino, an anthropologist at the Federal University of Santa Catarina who studies far-right politics online.

Jair, a far-right leader, is the father of this year’s presidential frontrunner, Flavio Bolsonaro.

When Jair first ran for president eight years ago, his platform promised tough-on-crime tactics and a return to traditional Christian family values, which he spread through bite-sized social media posts.

At his 2019 inauguration , supporters chanted “Facebook!” and “WhatsApp!” in unison to show their support for his online presence.

“Since then, the left and pro-democracy actors have slowly come to recognise the importance of such media for elections and learned how to deploy it strategically,” Cesarino told Al Jazeera.

“They still lag significantly behind the far right when it comes to digital communication, though, especially since the kind of logic that underlies the attention economy is structurally beneficial to the kind of alarmistic, simplistic, affect-laden far-right discourse.”

But during his presidential term, Jair used his social media platforms to cast doubt on the accuracy of Brazil’s election system.

After losing the 2022 election, Jair continued to spread false claims that the vote had been rigged. His supporters ultimately stormed three buildings – Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace – in the capital, Brasilia, on January 8, 2023, after Lula was sworn in.

In the aftermath, the TSE ruled that Jair had abused his position to undermine the election and prohibited him from holding public office for eight years.

He is currently serving a separate 27-year sentence for plotting a coup. He is also barred from using social media.

The scandal “really shocked a lot of policymakers and political elites to act”, said Vicky Wyatt, a campaign director at Eko, a coalition advocating for more accountability from tech companies.

Although Brazil had already passed some data privacy and data protection laws, leaders added a slew of new regulations after Jair’s presidency.

Brazilian law now bans depictions of electoral candidates generated by artificial intelligence (AI), and it also requires any political ads using AI to carry a disclaimer. Content that advocates violence, hate speech or gender-based discrimination is also considered illegal.

Only those with official campaign backing are supposed to be able to run ads on platforms like Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.

The country, said Wyatt, now has “some of the strictest laws in the world when it comes to guardrails around the use of AI on tech platforms”.

But those laws have been the source of pushback. In a statement to Al Jazeera, a Meta spokesperson framed the restrictions as a potential threat to free speech.

“Meta has long warned that Brazil’s strict digital-content rules increase the risk of over-enforcement and threaten free expression,” the company said.

Tech companies like Meta are supposed to walk regulators through their plans to comply with Brazil’s laws. However, evidence suggests Meta has not met its obligations.

Daniela da Silva, executive director of CTRL+Z, a nonprofit digital rights group, said some campaign coordinators have found their posts are not being shared as widely as they expected.

“They find their organic reach has decreased since the beginning of the elections, and they need to boost their posts,” da Silva told Al Jazeera. She added that some coordinators reported spending more than 70 percent of their budgets for such boosts on Meta.

As of October, CTRL+Z says it has collected 1,100 reports this year of accounts being taken down or having their reach restricted.

It determined that “the cases are mainly related to profiles supporting Lula”, who saw his own advertising account briefly suspended last month.

Lula’s campaign has cited studies by Eko, CTRL+Z and other groups to petition the TSE to intervene and enforce rules that require equal treatment for political campaigns.

Watchdog groups have also questioned whether social media platforms are complying with regulations that require them to remove false information and restrict AI-generated content.

One test, conducted by Eko, asked Meta to approve 15 election-season ads that included AI-generated content promoting violence and disinformation. In 13 cases, the social media platform approved them.

In another study, NetLab, a research group at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, found that Meta had allowed more than 1,600 political ads to run on its services, even though they were paid for by companies outside the country.

The group concluded that malicious actors appeared able to submit ads and tag them as non-political, allowing them to run on Meta’s services with little scrutiny, said Debora Gomes Salles, NetLab’s research head.

Meta made 2 million Brazilian reais ($400,000) from those ads, which, as far as Salles could tell, were meant to sow disinformation in the country.

Some told voters, for instance, that they could cast ballots online through a website that collected their private data. Voting online is not allowed at all in Brazil, Salles pointed out.

“Meta wasn’t really able to prevent these operations from happening, and even when it did do something and moderated this content, these ads were still a source of revenue for the company, and they already reached millions of Brazilians,” Salles said. “The damage was already done.”

Meta has repeatedly denied favouring any of this year’s presidential candidates on its platforms.

In a statement to Al Jazeera, a spokesperson said that technical errors were to blame for incidents like Lula’s campaign ads being taken offline temporarily.

The company also disputed the Eko report that suggested shortcomings in how it moderates campaign advertisements. The spokesperson said Meta’s system had correctly identified “content about social issues, elections or politics”.

“We removed ads that violated our policies,” the spokesperson said. The report’s small sample size, “out of millions in our Ad Library, does not reflect the scale of this work”.

Cesarino, the anthropologist who studies the far right online, said digital platforms will likely continue to spread problematic content.

The popularity of such content, she added, has contributed to the rise of far-right figures across the globe.

“It is not by chance that other far-right ‘populists’ rose at around the same time as Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, such as Donald Trump in the US or Narendra Modi in India,” Cesarino told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: How special executive magistrates play crucial role in deciding detentions
articles.summary: Special executive magistrates (SEMs) under BNSS can order peace bonds, remand or detention in preventive cases; their role and powers are under scrutiny in Delhi protests.
articles.body: New Delhi: Though a common feature in cases involving summary or preventive detention by police, the powers of special executive magistrates (SEMs) have come into focus due to their prominent role in deciding if those involved in recent protests rocking Delhi are released or remain behind bars.A person not familiar with the rare, overlapping functions and powers of the executive and judiciary may conclude SEMs are a rung of the judiciary where a person picked up by police is produced within 24 hours.However, the reality is more complex, since the law empowers govt officials, mostly police officers, to exercise magisterial powers in cases of detention, where they can even remand a detainee to judicial custody, as happened in the case of CJP’s Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka.Wednesday was the first time decisions taken by SEMs came under judicial scrutiny of any kind, when Delhi HC heard the CJP members’ plea. The court, however, refused to go into merits.Who are SEMs?Under Section 15 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), state govts can appoint executive magistrates or police officers of at least superintendent of police rank as SEMs for specific areas, periods or duties. Depending on state-specific notifications, these officers can also be deputy collectors or tehsildars or senior police officers of ACP rank. Their primary role is to take preventive measures to maintain public order and stop anticipated breaches of peace.How are they different from judicial magistrates?Under BNSS Section 9, the state govt establishes courts of judicial magistrates in consultation with HC, which appoints their presiding officers. Judicial magistrates deal with criminal cases and trials while SEMs exercise executive powers, including initiating preventive proceedings. SEMs cannot conduct criminal trials or convict people through these proceedings, but are authorised to release or grant police or judicial remand. Under the earlier Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), the corresponding provision for SEMs was Section 21.When can an SEM ask someone to furnish a peace bond?Under Section 126, an SEM can initiate proceedings if there is sufficient ground to believe a person is likely to breach the peace or disturb public tranquillity.*Procedure: Under Section 130, the magistrate must issue a written order explaining the basis for the proceedings, the proposed bond amount, its duration and the number of sureties required.*Duration: A peace bond can be required for up to one year, and the amount must not be excessive.*Can it be challenged? The person must be given an opportunity to explain why they should not be required to furnish the bond. The magistrate then conducts an inquiry under Section 135.Separately, Section 163 allows an executive magistrate to issue urgent orders to prevent specified dangers or disturbances, including restricting public gatherings when legal conditions are met.When can an SEM order detention?Detention is not automatic once proceedings begin.*During inquiry: Under Section 135(3), an SEM may require immediate security if necessary to prevent a breach of peace or danger to public safety. If the person fails to furnish it, they may be detained until the inquiry concludes.*After inquiry: Under Section 136, the magistrate can order security if the inquiry establishes it is necessary. Under Section 137, the person must be discharged if the need for security isn’t established.*Failure to furnish security: Section 141 provides for imprisonment in specified circumstances, including failure to furnish security after a final order or breach of a qualifying bond.Who can stand as a surety?A surety undertakes responsibility under a bond to help ensure the person concerned meets its conditions. Under Section 140, an SEM can reject a surety found unfit, but must conduct an inquiry, give the parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard and record reasons in writing.In Das and Ranka’s case, the SEM rejected fresh sureties over reported “discrepancies” in identification documents and missing details.• “Photograph mismatch”: The first surety’s photograph on the bond allegedly didn’t match his Aadhaar• “Insufficient identity proof”: He reportedly failed to produce another valid ID and gave unsatisfactory answers during questioning• “Lack of basic details”: The second surety couldn’t provide basic information, including the parentage and address of Saurav Das, for whom she stood as surety• “Insufficient control”: The SEM concluded the sureties didn’t have sufficient control over the activists to ensure their presence when requiredYou Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: Mizoram police seized 1.457 kg heroin worth Rs 2.914 crore in Saitual’s Keifang, arrested a 24-year-old Manipur man; probe into trafficking links underway.
articles.body: Aizawl: Police in Saitual district, bordering Manipur, seized 1.457 kg of heroin worth around Rs 2.914 crore at Keifang town and arrested a 24-year-old man from Manipur, Mizoram inspector general of police (IGP) and chief public relations officer H Ramthlengliana said on Wednesday.The IGP said a special team of the Saitual district police conducted random checks as part of its ongoing enforcement drive at the Kualmawi locality in Keifang town on Tuesday.The team intercepted a white car bearing an Assam registration number at 5.40 am. The vehicle was travelling from Manipur towards Aizawl and was driven by Thangminlun Baite of Manipur’s Kangpokpi district, Ramthlengliana said.Acting on suspicion that the vehicle was transporting illegal contraband, the police conducted a detailed search in the presence of independent witnesses. They seized 100 soap cases containing heroin, weighing a total of 1.457 kg and an estimated value of Rs 2.914 crore, the IGP said.The driver was arrested on the spot. Further investigation is underway to establish the drug network’s forward and backward linkages.Enforcement agencies said Champhai district, which borders Myanmar, remains the main route for drug trafficking from the Golden Triangle through Myanmar. articles.title: No selfish motive behind wearing RSS uniform: Rajendran
articles.summary: Former CPM MLA S Rajendran defends wearing RSS uniform at Munnar Vijayadashami, says BJP move wasn’t selfish and seeks solutions for Idukki land issues.
articles.body: Idukki: Former CPM MLA S Rajendran has hit back at criticism over his appearance in the RSS uniform at a Vijayadashami celebration in Munnar, saying that neither his decision to wear the uniform nor his move to BJP was motivated by personal interests. He said his objective was to stand with the people and work towards resolving long-standing problems facing Idukki.Rajendran’s appearance in full RSS uniform at the organisation’s Vijayadashami celebrations has triggered a political debate, particularly in view of his past association with CPM and his subsequent entry into BJP. He also inaugurated a publicity campaign for Kesari, the RSS-affiliated weekly, at the event.Responding to the criticism, Rajendran said he had never pursued politics for positions or financial benefits. He maintained that his decisions should be viewed in the context of his political journey and the issues affecting the people he had represented.“I did not wear the uniform out of selfishness. I joined BJP to stand with the people and work to resolve the problems of the region,” he said.The former MLA said critics should examine the circumstances that led to his political transition instead of judging his actions in isolation. He also pointed out that he had entered another political party after a gap of five years, urging those questioning his decision to take his public life and personal circumstances into account.‘Central intervention necessary to resolve land issues’Highlighting the challenges facing Idukki, Rajendran said intervention by the Central govt was essential to address issues concerning forest land and plantation areas. The region has been grappling with complex land-related issues that have affected residents and plantation communities.He acknowledged that his entry into BJP would not, by itself, guarantee solutions to these problems. However, he argued that efforts should be made to use the available political avenues to address the concerns of the people.Rajendran also rejected the suggestion that his decision to wear RSS uniform was intended to hurt anyone. He called for his actions to be assessed in the light of his political experience and the circumstances surrounding his career.From three-time CPM MLA to NDA candidateRajendran represented the Devikulam assembly constituency as a CPM candidate in 2006, 2011 and 2016, serving as MLA for 15 years. He also served as president of the Idukki district panchayat.His relationship with CPM subsequently deteriorated, eventually leading to his departure from the party. He joined BJP in Jan 2026 and later contested the Devikulam assembly constituency as NDA candidate in the 2026 election.His appearance in the RSS uniform marks another politically significant development in his transition from a long-time CPM legislator to a BJP member, bringing his political choices and stated commitment to resolving Idukki’s regional issues back into public discussion.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kochi | Silver Rate in Kochi | Bank Holidays in Kochi | Public Holidays in KochiStay updated with the latest Kochi news. articles.title: Judge orders Meta to pay $25 billion in trial related to 8-year-old data privacy scandal
articles.summary: A New Mexico state court has ordered Facebook-parent company Meta to pay a $25 billion penalty following a long legal battle stemming from the Cambridge
articles.body: A New Mexico state court has ordered Facebook-parent company Meta to pay a $25 billion penalty following a long legal battle stemming from the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal from nearly a decade ago. The judgment, revealed in a court filing on Wednesday (October 21), follows a September verdict by a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse. Jurors found the social media giant liable for deceiving New Mexico residents regarding how it gathers and safeguards personal data, as well as how it stops harmful content from spreading across its platforms.The jury determined that Meta committed more than 43 million individual violations of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act, each subject to a statutory civil fine of up to $5,000. However, the final penalty amount was left to judicial discretion. The ruling revealed that while the state was initially awarded $219.5 billion, the court reduced the ultimate penalty to $25 billion. In his filing, New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew delivered a rebuke of the company's past actions and internal practices, arguing that the maximum fine per violation was fully justified.“The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook’s repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury,” Judge Mathew wrote.Judge Mathew also ordered that the penalty will accrue interest at an annual rate of 15% until the judgment is settled in full.Internal inquiry was ‘Willfully Ineffective’The ruling pointed out that Facebook failed to live up to its public commitments following the 2018 Cambridge Analytica revelations, in which the political consultancy improperly gathered data belonging to an estimated 87 million users. Judge Mathew concluded that the tech firm “did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised.”Meta previously attempted to clear away nationwide litigation tied to the Cambridge Analytica fallout. In August, the tech giant agreed to an overarching $17 billion multi-state settlement with a coalition of state attorneys general in a broader federal lawsuit centered on child safety and mental health.However, as New Mexico chose not to join that nationwide pact, the state's independent Cambridge Analytica lawsuit proceeded directly to trial in September. The original complaint was initiated in 2021 by former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas, with current Attorney General Raúl Torrez directing the courtroom trial to its conclusion.You use AI every day. articles.title: Actors, writers condemn UK anti-terror law targeting Sally Rooney
articles.summary: Dozens of leading figures term the UK law banning Palestine Action a ‘repressive absurdity’.
articles.body:
Dozens of leading writers, actors and activists have condemned the UK law used to proscribe Palestine Action as a “repressive absurdity” in an open letter backing Irish novelist Sally Rooney, whose books have been withdrawn from sale in the United Kingdom.

The letter comes after Rooney said her books had been pulled from sale in the UK due to her public support for Palestine Action, a group the British government designated as a “terrorist organisation”.

Signatories include actors Paul Mescal – who played in an adaptation of her book Normal People, Susan Sarandon and Tilda Swinton; broadcaster Gary Lineker; and writers Arundhati Roy, Naomi Klein, JM Coetzee, Zadie Smith and William Dalrymple.

Filmmaker Jonathan Glazer, philosopher Slavoj Zizek, musician Kate Nash and the Irish hip-hop group Kneecap have also signed the letter.

“Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public,” the letter reads. “Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country.”

The letter appears on the cover of this week’s New Statesman magazine, two weeks before the Supreme Court is set to hear a case on the ban.

“We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity,” the letter concludes.

Rooney’s publisher, Faber & Faber, said on Wednesday that the withdrawal stemmed from “circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work” and to continue sales would be an “unconscionable situation for a publisher”.

Rooney has said that further publication of her work could constitute a “serious criminal offence”.

She said she had made “every effort to be honest” with the public about her beliefs and intentions, adding that she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”.

E-books of Rooney’s work have also been removed from sale in the UK, although some physical copies remain available in bookshops.

She has authored four best-selling novels, selling more than six million books globally.
